item.title: Kokusai-dori Guide: Shopping, Eats & Access (Naha)
item.description: Kokusai-dori (“International Street”) is Naha’s bustling main thoroughfare — a roughly 1.6 km stretch lined with souvenir shops, restaurants, izakaya, cafés and street performers. Rebuilt in the years after WWII and nicknamed the “Miracle Mile,” it’s the liveliest place in Okinawa to shop for local crafts and snacks, sample Okinawan cuisine, and feel the island’s easygoing energy. Dip into the covered market arcades just off the main drag for a more local, atmospheric experience.

item.title: Okinawa Soba Guide: What It Is, Where to Eat & Types
item.description: Despite the name, Okinawa soba contains no buckwheat — it’s a beloved local comfort food of thick, chewy wheat noodles in a clear, savoury pork-and-bonito broth, topped with tender pork, fish cake, pickled ginger and spring onion. Found everywhere from humble shokudo (diners) to dedicated specialists, it’s one of the first tastes of Okinawa most visitors fall for. Regional variations and toppings — from meaty soki to braised rafute — make it endlessly satisfying.

item.title: Taco Rice Guide: Okinawa's Tex-Mex Soul Food & Where to Eat
item.description: Taco rice is Okinawa’s quintessential fusion comfort food — seasoned taco-style ground beef, shredded lettuce, tomato and cheese piled over a bowl of white rice. Born near the American military bases in the 1980s as a cheap, filling meal for hungry servicemen, it crossed over into local life and is now an Okinawan icon. Hearty, cheap and crowd-pleasing, it’s a delicious window into the island’s deep American cultural layer. This guide covers its origins, what’s in it, where to eat it and how to order.
